extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers in communication/political science, and journalists/science communicators interested in how climate change is framed in news media
extracted.subtask_description: Automated and hand-coded content analysis of U.S. newspaper climate-change coverage, classifying articles for presence of specific frames (economic cost, economic benefit, conservative ideology, uncertainty) and measuring linguistic dimensions (risk language, present-tense). Uses supervised machine learning (SVM) and LIWC dictionary methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic Cost Frame
rubrics_metrics.description: We coded articles for whether (1) or not (0) they had references to economic costs for climate change mitigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These frames feature discussion of possible economic costs of mitigation (e.g., lost jobs, higher energy costs, impacts on businesses). Example: NYT coverage criticizing Kyoto for 'radically change[ing] the American life style.' Training/testing set: 1,878 articles. SVM classifier: ~80% accurate (average recall 0.76, precision 0.80). Note: analysis aggregates multiple distinct economic-cost dimensions under this umbrella.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic Benefit Frame
rubrics_metrics.description: We coded articles for whether (1) or not (0) they had references to economic benefits for climate change mitigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These frames emphasize win–win features of mitigation (green jobs, lower energy/gas bills via increased energy efficiency, increased profits). Important coding rule: discussion of energy efficiency alone did not meet criteria—there had to be mention of how such efficiency benefits consumers or companies in the long run. Example: WSJ story about Wal‑Mart saving money by reducing waste. Training/testing set: 864 articles. SVM classifier: ~80% accurate (average recall 0.74, precision 0.78).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative Ideological Frame
rubrics_metrics.description: We coded articles if there was any discussion related to conservative ideological themes (1) or not (0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically: arguments stressing opposition to climate action because policies empower bureaucrats, undermine American sovereignty, serve a 'big government' agenda, redistribute wealth, increase regulation, restrict freedom, or violate principles of the free market. Coding excluded conservative frames used in support of climate action (too rare). Examples include quotes calling accords an 'unprecedented government seizure of American freedom and sovereignty.' Training set: combined training/testing of 405 articles. Classifier accuracy ~85% (average recall 0.70, precision 0.80).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty / Balance toward IPCC Consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Each article was coded for how balanced it was toward arguments of supporters and opponents of the IPCC consensus (climate change is happening, manmade, serious). Original coding scale: −1 (no presence of discussion casting uncertainty on IPCC consensus), −0.5, 0, 0.5, 1 (complete rejection of IPCC consensus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because there were too few instances in intermediate categories, for automated training the categories above −1 were collapsed: articles were scored 1 if they had any discussion that cast doubt on the IPCC consensus (uncertainty frame), and 0 if they had no such discussion. Example: WP quote from George W. Bush illustrating 'wait and see' posture. Training/testing set: 1,179 articles. SVM classifier: 77% accurate (average recall 0.70, precision 0.68). Note: op-eds are the primary source of full rejection (score 1), while news stories often contain balanced/slightly slanted references (−0.5, 0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk Language (LIWC risk dictionary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk framing was measured with a dictionary method using LIWC's 'risk' dictionary (words/phrases such as alarm, avoid, hazard, threat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured as the percentage of words in an average article each year that indicate risk. Rationale: dictionary methods are straightforward and appropriate for simpler linguistic dimensions; LIWC provides pre‑assembled, validated dictionaries. Results: risk language usage increased over the study period (e.g., +35% from 1995 to 2014). Use of LIWC was chosen because supervised ML did not reliably capture these simpler linguistic aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present‑tense Language (LIWC present tense dictionary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal distance coding used LIWC's present‑tense dictionary (words like lives, now, present) to measure present-tense language in coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured as frequency/proportion of present-tense words per article; used to infer temporal framing (focus on 'here and now' vs. distant future). Results show increased present-tense usage around mid‑2000s. Rationale: dictionary approach is appropriate for capturing tense reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological choice: supervised ML (SVM) vs dictionary methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Supervised machine learning (SVM) was used to classify substantive frames (economic cost/benefit, conservative ideology, uncertainty) because dictionary approaches failed to reliably capture those complex frames; dictionary methods (LIWC) were used for simpler linguistic dimensions (risk, tense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: frames were difficult to capture with inductively created dictionaries, while supervised ML trained on hand-coded examples performed reliably. The paper reports training/testing set sizes and classifier performance for each frame (see classifier performance entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifier performance metrics (accuracy, recall, precision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance of SVM classifiers for each coded frame as reported in the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic cost classifier: 80% accurate, average recall 0.76, precision 0.80. Economic benefit classifier: 80% accurate, average recall 0.74, precision 0.78. Conservative ideology classifier: 85% accurate, average recall 0.70, precision 0.80. Uncertainty classifier: 77% accurate, average recall 0.70, precision 0.68. These metrics are used to assess reliability of automated coding and to compare SVM results to manual coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand coding reliability (Krippendorff's alpha / coder validation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manual coding process and inter‑coder reliability metrics used to validate training labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One researcher completed hand coding; a second randomly selected 10% (200 articles) to assess reliability. Reported Krippendorff's alpha: economic cost frames 0.87 (95% agreement), economic benefit frames 0.92 (98% agreement), uncertainty frames 0.88 (96% agreement), conservative frames 0.83 (99% agreement). This level of reliability underpins the supervised ML training data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring policy: collapsing fine‑grained balance categories for training
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational decision due to sparse data in some balance categories: collapsed all categories above −1 when training the algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a result, the automated classifier treated articles as binary for uncertainty: 1 if any discussion cast doubt on IPCC consensus, 0 if none. Rationale: too few instances of articles scored 0 and below to train a reliable fine‑grained measure of article balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corpus composition and temporal windows
rubrics_metrics.description: Design of corpus used for the study: outlets, time periods, and source composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main sources: Associated Press (AP), New York Times (NYT), Washington Post (WP), Wall Street Journal (WSJ). Time periods: Period 1 (1988–1996), Period 2 (1997–2005), Period 3 (2006–2014). Training/testing sets were pulled from a larger number of mainstream newspapers (only ~30% of the training set came from other mainstream newspapers). Purpose: to analyze prevalence and change over time across outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: aggregation of economic-frame subdimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that coding distinct dimensions of economic frames together within umbrellas of 'economic costs' and 'economic benefits' may lose nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example limitation: cannot determine whether disemployment effects are more common than energy-cost frames. Authors recommend more thorough human coding in future work to tease out different subdimensions to capture nuance lost by aggregation for automated analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: False balance assessment (operationalization and interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of 'false balance' in media coverage via presence of uncertainty framing and distribution across article types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationally: any uncertainty framing counts toward false balance measures; findings indicate false balance is rare and declining, with full rejections concentrated in op‑eds rather than news stories. Authors note that even their estimates are liberal and that AP wire coverage shows particularly low uncertainty framing. Implication: measuring false balance requires attention to article type (news vs op‑ed) and source practices.
